predecessors.name: Warring States Japan
predecessors.text: Echigo Province (Niigata Prefecture; the shape also takes in Sado, which the pages do not mention)

successors.name: Japan (Empire of Japan, 1868-1947)
successors.text: Yonezawa after 1664: the 150,000 koku Dewa portion

ledger.x: 1548: Kenshin 'succeeded in wresting control of the Nagao clan from Nagao Harukage in 1548' and 'ruled Echigo Province'.
1553: Kawanakajima.
Fall 1560: the Kantō campaign.
Summer 1561: the campaign ends.
1561: Numata and Umayabashi Castles taken from the Hōjō.
1563: 'Kenshin occupied Sano Domain of Kōzuke Province'.
1564: the fifth and last Kawanakajima; the page gives no treaty.
1565: Shingen 'took Kuragano and Minowa Castles in Kōzuke'.

1570: Etchū. Kenshin 'first entered the dispute as a mediator in the early 1560s'; he took the Shiina's 'main castle in 1570'. The extent of the holding is the researcher's reading (the whole province).
1577: Noto. 'Eventually in 1577, Kenshin secured and controlled the Noto and Kaga Province from the Oda clan'; the infobox dates the siege of Nanao 1576 and 1577.
1577: Kaga, in the same sentence as Noto.
1578: the succession after Kenshin died.
1579: Kagetora 'is forced to commit suicide'; the succession is closed.
1579: the clan's division 'let Oda Nobunaga's generals take Uesugi lands in Kaga, Noto and Etchū'.
3 June 1582: Oda forces defeat Kagekatsu at Tenjinyama in Etchū and Uozu Castle falls.
1598: Hideyoshi 'redistributes holdings' and Kagekatsu receives Aizu.
1598: Kagekatsu 'receives Aizu', valued at 1.2 million koku.
1601: the Uesugi 'keep only Yonezawa', 300,000 koku of the 1,200,000.
1601: Yonezawa Domain, established 1601; Kagekatsu is lord of Yonezawa from 1601.
1601: Yonezawa Castle is the seat.
1664: the third daimyo died without an heir, the domain 'is split', leaving 'only the 150,000 koku portion within Dewa province'.
1868: Yonezawa 'joins the Northern Alliance during the Boshin War'; the page names no battle on Uesugi land.
1869: the Meiji government cut the domain by 40,000 koku; the page gives no surrender, so the end is bridged from the punishment.
1871: 'the han system is abolished' and the domain becomes Yonezawa Prefecture, later merged with Okitama Prefecture into Yamagata Prefecture.

wars.name: Battles of Kawanakajima
wars.outcome: Five battles (1553, 1555, 1557, 1561, 1564) without a decision; the Takeda kept Shinano, the Uesugi stayed in Echigo.

wars.name: Uesugi Kantō campaign against the Hōjō
wars.outcome: Numata and Umayabashi were taken in 1560-1561 and Sano in 1563; the first siege of Odawara in 1561 failed.

wars.name: Uesugi–Oda war in Etchū, Noto and Kaga
wars.outcome: Kenshin took Noto and Kaga in 1577 (Tedorigawa fought in Kaga); the Oda took them back and beat Kagekatsu at Tenjinyama in Etchū, Uozu fell on 3 June 1582.

wars.name: Otate no Ran (Uesugi succession war)
wars.outcome: Kagekatsu beat Kagetora at the siege of Otate in 1578; Kagetora was forced to suicide in 1579.

wars.name: Sekigahara campaign in the north
wars.outcome: Kagekatsu was beaten at the sieges of Shiroishi and Hasedo; Uesugi holdings fell from 1,200,000 to 300,000 koku and the house kept Yonezawa.

wars.name: Boshin War (Yonezawa in the Northern Alliance)
wars.outcome: Yonezawa joined the Northern Alliance in 1868; in 1869 the Meiji government cut the domain by 40,000 koku.

certainty.note: The pages name castles, provinces and koku, not borders; the Echigo, Etchū, Noto, Aizu and Yonezawa shapes are the researcher's stand-ins.
